title: Introduction to Biology — Scope and Fields
topicTitle: Introduction to Biology: scope and fields of biology
notes: **Biology:** the scientific study of living organisms and their interactions with each other and their environment.

**Major branches:** botany (plants), zoology (animals), microbiology (microorganisms), genetics (inheritance), ecology (environment), evolution (change over time), physiology (function), biochemistry (molecular basis).
**Levels of organisation:** molecular → cellular → tissue → organ → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.
**Scope:** includes medicine, agriculture, biotechnology, environmental conservation, forensic science, and bioinformatics.
**Relation to other sciences:** biology uses chemistry (biochemistry), physics (biophysics), mathematics (biostatistics), and geology (palaeontology).
**Botany sub-disciplines:** phycology (algae), bryology (mosses), pteridology (ferns), mycology (fungi), paleobotany (fossil plants), plant anatomy, plant physiology, plant taxonomy.

**Zoology sub-disciplines:** entomology (insects), ornithology (birds), mammalogy (mammals), herpetology (reptiles and amphibians), ichthyology (fish), embryology (development), ethology (animal behaviour), comparative anatomy.
**Microbiology sub-disciplines:** bacteriology (bacteria), virology (viruses), mycology (fungi), protozoology (protozoa), phycology (algae), immunology (immune system).

**Genetics:** studies heredity and variation. Includes molecular genetics (DNA structure/function), population genetics (allele frequency changes), quantitative genetics (polygenic traits), and cytogenetics (chromosome behaviour).

**Ecology:** studies interactions between organisms and their environment. Sub-fields: autecology (individual species), synecology (communities), landscape ecology, restoration ecology, conservation biology.

**Evolution:** Darwin's theory of natural selection explains adaptation and speciation. Modern synthesis combines genetics with natural selection. Evidence comes from fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biogeography, and molecular biology.

**Physiology:** study of functions and mechanisms in living systems. Human physiology covers organ systems (circulatory, respiratory, nervous, digestive, excretory, endocrine, reproductive). Comparative physiology examines adaptations across species.

**Taxonomy and systematics:** taxonomy classifies organisms; systematics studies evolutionary relationships. Three-domain system: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya. Linnaean hierarchy: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

**Molecular biology:** studies biological molecules — DNA, RNA, proteins. Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein. Techniques include PCR, gel electrophoresis, Southern/Northern blotting, CRISPR gene editing.

**Cell biology:** studies cell structure and function. Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, chloroplasts (in plants). Cell theory: all living things are made of cells; cells are basic unit of life; all cells come from pre-existing cells.

**Biotechnology applications:** medicine (gene therapy, monoclonal antibodies, recombinant vaccines), agriculture (GMOs, tissue culture, marker-assisted breeding), industry (enzymes, biofuels, bioplastics), environment (bioremediation, wastewater treatment).
**Biomedical science:** applies biological principles to medicine. Includes pathology, pharmacology, hematology, radiology, and clinical diagnostics.
**Agricultural biology:** crop improvement, plant breeding, soil science, agronomy, horticulture, animal husbandry, fisheries science, entomology for pest management.
**Marine biology:** study of ocean ecosystems. Includes pelagic zone organisms, coral reef ecology, deep-sea vent communities, tidal zone adaptation, and marine conservation.

**Developmental biology:** studies how organisms grow and develop from a single cell (zygote) into a multicellular adult. Key concepts: differentiation, morphogenesis, pattern formation, and stem cell biology.
**Neurobiology:** studies the nervous system — neurons, synapses, neural circuits, brain function, and behaviour. Bridges cell biology, physiology, and psychology.
**Immunology:** studies the immune system — innate immunity (barriers, phagocytes, inflammation) and adaptive immunity (B cells, T cells, antibodies, immunological memory).

**Virology:** studies viruses — structure (capsid, envelope, genome type), replication cycles (lytic vs. lysogenic), host interaction, and viral evolution. Viruses sit at the boundary of living and non-living.
**Chronobiology:** studies biological rhythms — circadian rhythms (24-hour cycles), seasonal cycles, and tidal cycles. Regulated by internal biological clocks and external cues (light, temperature).
**Space biology (astrobio-related):** studies how life responds to space conditions — microgravity effects on growth, radiation damage to DNA, and potential for life in extraterrestrial environments.
**Conservation biology:** an applied discipline that uses ecology, genetics, and population biology to prevent species extinction, maintain biodiversity, and restore degraded ecosystems.
**Paleobiology:** combines paleontology and biology to study extinct organisms — their anatomy, ecology, evolution, and extinction events (e.g., the K-Pg extinction that wiped out dinosaurs).

**Phylogenetics and cladistics:** phylogenetics reconstructs evolutionary relationships using molecular and morphological data; cladistics groups organisms by shared derived characteristics (synapomorphies) into monophyletic clades. Phylogenetic trees are built using maximum parsimony, maximum likelihood, and Bayesian methods.

**Evo-devo (evolutionary developmental biology):** studies how changes in developmental genes (Hox genes, signaling pathways) produce evolutionary change. Explains how similar body plans arise across diverse animals and how developmental processes can be co-opted for novel structures.

**Structural biology:** determines 3D structures of biological macromolecules using X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM (electron microscopy), and NMR spectroscopy. Understanding structure explains function — enzyme active sites, drug-receptor interactions, and molecular machines.

**Systems biology:** takes a holistic approach to biological systems, integrating genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics data to model complex interactions. Uses computational modeling to understand emergent properties that reductionist approaches miss.

**Astrobiology:** studies the origin, evolution, distribution, and future of life in the universe. Combines biology, astronomy, geology, and chemistry. Focus areas: extremophiles as analogs for extraterrestrial life, biosignature detection, planetary protection, and the habitable zone concept.

**Ethology and behavioural ecology:** studies animal behaviour from evolutionary and ecological perspectives. Key concepts: Tinbergen's four questions (causation, development, function, evolution), optimal foraging theory, kin selection (inclusive fitness), and game theory in animal conflict.

**Biomechanics:** applies principles of mechanics to biological systems. Studies locomotion (swimming, flying, walking), skeletal mechanics, muscle physiology, fluid dynamics in circulatory and respiratory systems, and the physics of sensory organs.

**Nephrology and comparative excretion:** studies excretory systems across organisms. Protonephridia (flatworms) use flame cells; metanephridia (annelids) collect coelomic fluid; Malpighian tubules (insects) excrete waste into hindgut; kidneys (vertebrates) filter blood via glomeruli. Osmoregulation maintains internal solute balance.

**Sensory biology and neuroecology:** studies how organisms detect and process environmental information. Special senses (electroreception in sharks, magnetoreception in birds, infrared detection in pit vipers) and general senses (mechanoreception, chemoreception, photoreception). Neural coding translates stimuli into perception.

**Population biology and life history theory:** studies population dynamics (growth, regulation, carrying capacity) and life history strategies (r-selected vs. K-selected species). Trade-offs between reproduction, growth, and survival shape evolutionary fitness. Matrix population models predict long-term growth rates.

**Biogeochemistry and nutrient cycling:** biology drives global cycles of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and water. Photosynthesis fixes carbon; nitrogen fixation converts N2 to ammonia; decomposition recycles nutrients. Human activity has dramatically altered these cycles through fossil fuel burning, fertilizer use, and land conversion.

**Regeneration and stem cell biology:** some organisms (planarians, axolotls) can regenerate entire body parts through dedifferentiation and stem cell proliferation. Mammalian stem cells (embryonic, adult, iPSCs) maintain tissue homeostasis and offer therapeutic potential. Wound healing in humans involves similar but limited regenerative processes.

**Bioluminescence and biofluorescence:** living organisms produce light through chemical reactions (luciferin-luciferase in fireflies, coelenterazine in marine organisms) or absorb and re-emit light (GFP in jellyfish). Functions include predation (anglerfish lure), mating (firefly signals), camouflage (counter-illumination in squid), and warning coloration.

**Extremophiles and their applications:** organisms thriving in extreme conditions — thermophiles (hot springs, hydrothermal vents), halophiles (salt lakes), acidophiles (acid mine drainage), barophiles (deep ocean), psychrophiles (Antarctic ice). Their enzymes (extremozymes) have industrial applications: Taq polymerase from thermophiles, cold-adapted enzymes for detergents.

**Epigenetics:** heritable changes in gene expression without altering DNA sequence. Mechanisms include DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA. Epigenetic marks respond to environmental factors (diet, stress, toxins) and can be passed across generations. Critical in development, cancer, and transgenerational inheritance.
confusion: Do not confuse this concept with similar-sounding terms. Check definitions carefully.
Always verify the conditions under which the formula applies — many formulas have restricted domains.
Sign conventions matter. Define your coordinate system before applying equations.
Taxonomy is classification; systematics is about evolutionary relationships — they overlap but are not identical.
Physiology studies HOW things work (function); anatomy studies WHAT things are (structure).
Microbiology is not just bacteria — it includes viruses, fungi, protozoa, and algae.
Evolution is NOT progress toward perfection; it is change in heritable traits over generations driven by natural selection, drift, mutation, and gene flow.

Botany is not simply 'plant biology' — it is a formal discipline with its own sub-fields (phycology, bryology, etc.), whereas plant biology is a broader term that can include molecular approaches across all plant sciences.

Biotechnology is not the same as genetic engineering — genetic engineering is one tool within biotechnology; biotechnology also includes traditional techniques like fermentation and selective breeding.

Ecology is not the same as environmental science — ecology is specifically about organism-environment interactions, while environmental science is an interdisciplinary field that also includes chemistry, policy, and economics.

Phylogenetics and systematics are closely related but distinct — systematics is the broader study of evolutionary relationships, while phylogenetics is the specific methodology of reconstructing those relationships using data.
Evo-devo is not just developmental biology — it specifically asks how developmental processes have evolved and how changes in development produce evolutionary novelty.
Extremophiles are not the same as pathogens of extreme environments — extremophiles thrive IN extreme conditions, while pathogens cause disease in hosts regardless of environmental extremity.
Bioluminescence (chemical light production) is distinct from biofluorescence (absorbing and re-emitting light) and biophosphorescence (delayed light emission without continuous input).
Epigenetics is NOT genetic mutation — epigenetic changes affect gene expression without changing the DNA sequence itself, though they can be heritable.
practice: Solve one basic problem using the key formula from this topic.
Try a numerical problem where you must choose the correct formula from two similar options.
Apply this concept to a real-world situation and explain each step.
List all levels of biological organisation from smallest to largest and give one example at each level.
Classify the following organisms into the three-domain system and justify your choices: E. coli, yeast, human, cyanobacteria, archaea from hot springs.
Explain how a single organism can be studied at every level of organisation from molecule to biosphere, using a human or a tree as an example.
Map out which biological sub-disciplines would be involved in studying a coral reef ecosystem, from molecular to ecosystem level.
Distinguish between taxonomy and systematics using the classification of humans (Homo sapiens) as an example. What does each tell you?
A new species of deep-sea fish is discovered. Describe the biological sub-disciplines you would consult to fully understand it.
Explain why virology is controversial as a branch of biology, given that viruses do not meet all criteria of life.

Construct a phylogenetic tree for five organisms (human, chimpanzee, rat, chicken, yeast) using morphological and molecular evidence. Explain which branching pattern is most supported by current data.
Design an experiment to determine whether a newly discovered deep-sea organism is a producer, consumer, or decomposer. What biological disciplines would you employ?
Explain how the study of extremophiles has expanded our understanding of the limits of life and implications for astrobiology. Give three specific examples of extremophiles and their environments.
Compare r-selected and K-selected life history strategies using real organisms. How do environmental conditions determine which strategy is advantageous?
Trace the carbon atom from CO2 in the atmosphere through photosynthesis, consumption, respiration, and decomposition. Which biological disciplines are relevant at each step?
universalFacts: This concept is fundamental and appears in multiple contexts across the subject.
Understanding the derivation helps more than memorizing the final formula.
Always check units and dimensions when applying this concept.
Biology is uniquely interdisciplinary — no other science touches so many other fields in everyday practice.
The hierarchy of biological organisation (molecule → biosphere) is a recurring framework used across all biology courses.
Every branch of biology shares the same core themes: evolution, energy flow, information transfer, and homeostasis.
The number of described species is estimated at 1.5–2 million, but total species (including undescribed) may exceed 8–10 million.
Biology is the only science that studies its own origins — life arose from non-living matter through chemical evolution.
All known life on Earth shares the same genetic code, suggesting a single common ancestor for all organisms.
The deepest branches of the tree of life are occupied by prokaryotes (Bacteria and Archaea), which diverged over 3 billion years ago.
Biology has more sub-disciplines than any other science — over 150 recognized branches — reflecting the extraordinary diversity of life.
The same fundamental molecules (DNA, RNA, proteins, lipids, carbohydrates) are used by every known organism, from bacteria to blue whales.
Biology is experiencing a data revolution: the amount of biological data doubles roughly every 2 years, driven by sequencing, imaging, and computational tools.
